title: Overview and justification
body:
This course is about succeeding at university as you reach the end of your degree. Succeeding is more than good marks. It is learning to direct your own study, building the capital a graduate carries into work and life, and being able to say, with evidence, what you have become. By the end you will be able to appraise how self-regulated learning and self-efficacy sustain your success, evaluate the graduate capital you are building across its five forms, and define success on your own terms.

At this stage the question is no longer how to start. It is how to own and articulate what you are already doing. Employers, interview panels and your own plans all ask you to make your development explicit. This course helps you name it.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this course, you will be able to:

_items.text: appraise how self-regulated learning and self-efficacy sustain success at university
evaluate the graduate capital you are building across its five forms
define and articulate success on your own terms as you become a graduate.

title: In real academic practice
body: Succeeding at university is the rehearsal for succeeding beyond it. The habits of a self-regulating learner, the capital you build, and the ability to articulate your development are exactly what graduate recruiters, professional bodies and research supervisors look for. The work you do here is the work of becoming a graduate, not a bolt-on to it.

title: Signpost
body: The course has three short lessons. First, the engine of succeeding: self-regulated learning and self-efficacy, the resources that keep you going. Second, graduate capital: the framework that reframes success and its five forms. Third, defining success and becoming a graduate: setting your own terms and articulating what you can evidence. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

title: How this course works
body:
The examples and activities in this course use invented people, authors and sources to show how things work. Unless we say otherwise, any name, citation or reference you meet in an example is fictional.

Where a lesson draws on real work, you'll find it listed under Lesson Sources at the bottom of that page. Every real source used in the course is gathered under Course Sources at the end.

title: Confidence check
instruction: Before you start, rate how confident you feel about each statement. There are no right or wrong answers.
_preConfirmation: Thank you. You will see these statements again at the end of the course, so you can see how your confidence has changed.

_items.text: I can appraise how self-regulated learning and self-efficacy sustain my success at university.
I can evaluate the graduate capital I am building across its five forms.
I can define and articulate success on my own terms as I become a graduate.

title: Orientation
body: By this point in your degree you have a way of working. This lesson asks you to look at the engine behind it. Students who succeed are not simply the ones who work hardest; they are the ones who regulate their own learning, setting direction, monitoring progress and adjusting. This lesson names that engine and the belief that keeps it running.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are near the end of your studies, so the aim is not to learn these ideas for the first time. It is to recognise them in how you already work, appraise how well they are serving you, and be able to explain them to someone else, such as an interviewer. That articulation is the advanced step.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain how self-regulated learning and academic literacies underpin success at this stage
appraise the part self-efficacy plays in sustaining your effort through difficulty
judge whether a student working in {{context}} is regulating their own learning.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Self-regulated learning is the process by which you take charge of your own study: setting goals, choosing strategies, monitoring how it is going, and adjusting when it is not. It is more than organisation. It is a cycle of planning, doing and reflecting that you run for yourself, rather than waiting to be directed. Alongside it sit academic literacies: the ways of reading, writing and thinking a discipline expects, which are far more than a set of study skills.

Self-efficacy is your belief that you can succeed at a particular task. It is built mainly through mastery, the experience of overcoming a challenge, and it is fed by seeing others like you succeed, by honest encouragement, and by keeping stress in check. Self-efficacy matters because it governs how long you persist when work gets hard, which is exactly when success is decided.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a time your work was not going well. Did you keep doing the same thing, or did you monitor and change it? What is one strategy you could switch to next time, and what small win would tell you it is working?

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Succeeding rests on an engine: self-regulated learning, the habit of directing your own study by setting goals, monitoring progress and adjusting, supported by the academic literacies your discipline expects. Self-efficacy is the belief that keeps that engine running when work gets hard, and it is built mostly through small mastery experiences. You can now explain this engine, appraise the part self-efficacy plays, and judge whether a student is really regulating their learning. The next lesson names what all this effort is building: your graduate capital.

title: Orientation
body: You now know the engine. This lesson names what it produces. A degree does not only raise your marks; it builds capital you carry into everything after. Michael Tomlinson called this graduate capital, and his framework is a way of seeing your whole degree as an investment in five kinds of resource, not just a transcript.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: The advanced move here is not to memorise five labels. It is to hold the framework up against your own degree and work out, honestly, which forms you are building and which you are neglecting. That evaluation is exactly what a strong graduate application or interview answer is made of.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain what graduate capital is and how it reframes success beyond marks
distinguish the five forms of graduate capital from one another
evaluate which forms of graduate capital you are building in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Graduate capital is the idea that a degree builds more than knowledge. It builds resources you can draw on in work and life. Michael Tomlinson set out this framework in 2017, and it reframes the question from what marks did I get to what have I become able to do, know and be.

The five forms are human capital, social capital, cultural capital, identity capital and psychological capital. Each names a different resource your degree can build, and the activity below unpacks each one. A successful graduate has built across all five, not banked marks alone.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Of the five forms of graduate capital, which have you built most strongly during your degree, and which have you neglected? What is one thing you could do before you graduate to strengthen the weakest one?

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Graduate capital reframes success as the resources a degree builds, not marks alone. Tomlinson's framework names five forms: human, social, cultural, identity and psychological capital. You can now explain why this reframes success, distinguish the five forms, and evaluate which ones your own degree is building and which you are neglecting. The final lesson brings this back to you: defining success on your own terms and articulating what you can evidence.

title: Orientation
body: The course ends where a degree ends: with the question of what success has meant. The book splits success two ways, into academic performance and personal development, and most students chase only the first. This lesson asks you to define success on your own terms, using both, and to practise articulating the development you can evidence as you become a graduate.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this level, defining success is not a warm-up exercise; it is the thing itself. Being able to state, with evidence, what you set out to achieve and what you have become is the articulation employers, funders and you yourself will ask for. This lesson is deliberately about your own case, not a generic one.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: distinguish success as academic performance from success as personal development
define success on your own terms, drawing on both kinds
articulate the development in {{context}} you can evidence as you become a graduate.

title: Concept: definition
body:
The book defines success in two ways. Success as academic performance is about results: grades, marks, and the steps you take towards mastering your subject. Success as personal development is about who you become: the confidence, independence, adaptability and other graduate attributes you grow along the way. Both are real success, and the two often grow together.

Defining success on your own terms means deciding, deliberately, what a good outcome looks like for you across both kinds, rather than inheriting a single measure such as a grade. As you become a graduate, the final skill is articulation: being able to say, with evidence, what you set out to do, what you achieved, and what you can now do. That articulation is how success is recognised by others.

title: Reflective prompt
body: In a sentence or two, define what success in your degree has meant to you, drawing on both your performance and how you have developed. Then name one piece of evidence you could use to articulate it to someone else.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Success at university comes in two kinds: academic performance, your results, and personal development, who you become. Defining success on your own terms means setting a good outcome across both, rather than inheriting a single measure. As you become a graduate, the decisive skill is articulation: saying, with evidence, what you set out to do and what you can now do. With the engine of self-regulated learning, the language of graduate capital, and your own definition of success, you are ready to say what succeeding has meant for you.

title: Course summary
body: You have reached the end of the course. Succeeding at university is no longer just a grade. You can appraise the engine behind it, self-regulated learning sustained by self-efficacy. You can evaluate the graduate capital your degree is building across its five forms. And you can define success on your own terms and articulate, with evidence, what you have become. Look back at the confidence check: comparing where you started with where you are now shows how far this has moved.

title: In real academic practice
body: From here, these are not study ideas but working habits. Every application you write, every interview you sit, every supervision or appraisal you attend, asks you to regulate your own work, show the capital you bring, and articulate your development with evidence. The course has rehearsed exactly that. Succeeding at university and succeeding beyond it draw on the same moves.

definition: Taking charge of your own study by setting goals, choosing strategies, monitoring progress, and adjusting as you go.
extendedDefinition: A self-regulated learner runs the cycle of planning, doing and reflecting for themselves, rather than waiting to be directed. This is the habit that most reliably separates students who succeed from those who simply work hard. It is the engine every other skill in this course depends on.
example: Noticing that re-reading is not working, a self-regulated learner switches to testing themselves, then checks whether their marks improve.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two final-year students hit the same wall: a module whose reading they find genuinely hard.

{{learner-a}} keeps doing what has always worked, reading the chapter again and again, and getting the same blank result. When the mark comes back low, {{learner-a}} concludes the module is simply too difficult and eases off. The effort was there, but nothing was monitored or changed, and the belief that it could be cracked drained away.

{{learner-b}} hits the same wall but treats it as information. {{learner-b}} notices the re-reading is not working, switches to writing summary questions and testing against them, and checks whether the next seminar goes better. It does, a little, and that small win rebuilds the confidence to keep going. This is self-regulated learning with self-efficacy intact.

Both students worked hard. Only {{learner-b}} regulated the learning, monitoring what was happening and adjusting, and protected the belief that persistence would pay.

title: Regulating your own learning
displayTitle: Checklist: How to do it
body: These moves turn self-regulated learning from an idea into something you do. Try them on a piece of work that is not going well.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I set a specific goal for this task, not just an intention to work on it?
Have I chosen a strategy on purpose, rather than defaulting to what I always do?
Have I checked, partway through, whether the strategy is actually working?
Have I changed approach when the evidence said the first one was not working?
Have I noticed and banked a small win to protect my belief that I can do this?
Have I reflected afterwards on what to carry into the next task?

title: Formative check: the engine of succeeding
displayTitle: Which statement best captures what self-regulated learning adds to simply working hard?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does self-regulated learning add to working hard?

_items.text: Directing your own study: setting goals, monitoring progress, and changing strategy when needed.
_items.feedback: Yes. Regulating your learning means steering it, not just putting hours in.

_items.text: Spending more hours on the task than anyone else in your group.
_items.feedback: Hours alone are effort, not regulation; the point is steering the effort.

_items.text: Following the reading list in the exact order it is given.
_items.feedback: Following a list is compliance, not self-regulation of your learning.

_items.text: Waiting for the tutor to tell you what to do next.
_items.feedback: Waiting to be directed is the opposite of regulating your own learning.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Self-regulated learning steers your study: goals, monitoring and adjustment, not just more hours.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about steering your own study rather than adding effort or waiting for direction.
_incorrect.final: Self-regulated learning means directing your own study and adjusting it. Extra hours, fixed lists and waiting for direction are not regulation.

title: Formative check: self-efficacy and persistence
displayTitle: In the worked example, what best explains why the second student kept going when the first gave up?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why did the second student keep going?

_items.text: A small win rebuilt their self-efficacy, the belief that persistence would pay off.
_items.feedback: Yes. Mastery experiences rebuild the belief that keeps effort going.

_items.text: They were naturally more intelligent than the first student.
_items.feedback: The example turns on what they did, not on fixed ability.

_items.text: They had less difficult reading to get through.
_items.feedback: Both students faced the same hard reading; the difference was how they responded.

_items.text: They spent far longer on the task overall.
_items.feedback: The difference was monitoring and a rebuilt belief, not extra time.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A small mastery experience rebuilt self-efficacy, and that belief sustained the effort.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for what changed the second student's belief that the work could be cracked.
_incorrect.final: The second student kept going because a small win rebuilt their self-efficacy. Ability, easier reading and extra time are not what the example turns on.

title: Formative check: judging self-regulation
displayTitle: A student working in {{context}} keeps missing a target and repeats the same approach each time, then concludes the subject is too hard. What is missing?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What is missing from the student's approach?

_items.text: Self-regulation: nothing is monitored, and no strategy is changed.
_items.feedback: Yes. In {{context}}, regulating your learning means monitoring and adjusting, which this student never does.

_items.text: Nothing; repeating the same approach is the disciplined thing to do.
_items.feedback: Repeating an approach that is not working is not discipline; it skips monitoring.

_items.text: More raw effort; they simply need to try harder.
_items.feedback: They are already trying; what is missing is monitoring and a change of strategy.

_items.text: A better timetable for the week ahead.
_items.feedback: A timetable organises time but does not monitor or adjust the strategy.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, the student is not regulating their learning: nothing is monitored and no strategy changes.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for what a self-regulated learner does that this student does not.
_incorrect.final: What is missing is self-regulation: monitoring progress and changing strategy. More effort, more discipline or a timetable do not supply it.

title: Information cards
displayTitle: The five forms of graduate capital
body: Each card is one form of capital your degree can build. Review all five.
instruction: Read through the cards below.
ariaRegion: Information cards describing the five forms of graduate capital.

_items.title: Human capital
_items.subtitle: Knowledge and skills
_items.text: The subject expertise and transferable skills your degree gives you, from writing and analysis to lab or studio technique.

_items.title: Social capital
_items.subtitle: Networks and relationships
_items.text: The connections you build with peers, tutors, mentors and professionals, and your ability to draw on them well.

_items.title: Cultural capital
_items.subtitle: Knowing how the field works
_items.text: Understanding how your profession behaves and communicates, so you can read its codes and act credibly within it.

_items.title: Identity capital
_items.subtitle: Who you are becoming
_items.text: A clear, evidenced sense of your professional self: your values, your direction and the story you can tell about them.

_items.title: Psychological capital
_items.subtitle: Resilience and belief
_items.text: The self-efficacy, optimism and resilience to cope with setbacks and keep adapting, carried over from the first lesson.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students reach the end of the same degree with similar marks, and both are asked in interview what they have gained.

{{learner-a}} talks only about modules passed and the final grade. It is accurate, but it is all human capital, and only the paper kind. The panel learns what {{learner-a}} studied, not what {{learner-a}} can offer an organisation, who they can work with, or how they handle setbacks.

{{learner-b}} gives the grade, then adds more: a group project that built a professional network, a placement that showed how the field actually operates, and a hard second year that proved their resilience. {{learner-b}} is describing human, social, cultural and psychological capital together, with an identity to tie them up.

Both earned the degree. Only {{learner-b}} could evaluate it across the five forms, and so made the stronger case.

title: Auditing your graduate capital
displayTitle: Checklist: How to do it
body: Use these prompts to evaluate the graduate capital your own degree is building. Be honest about the gaps.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Human capital: can I name specific skills and knowledge, not just modules I passed?
Social capital: have I built relationships with peers, staff or professionals I could draw on?
Cultural capital: do I understand how my field actually works and communicates?
Identity capital: can I say clearly who I am becoming professionally, and why?
Psychological capital: can I point to a setback I coped with and adapted to?
Overall: which form am I neglecting, and what could I do before I graduate to build it?

title: Formative check: what graduate capital reframes
displayTitle: What does the idea of graduate capital add to judging success by marks alone?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does graduate capital add to judging success by marks?

_items.text: It counts the wider resources a degree builds, such as networks, resilience and professional identity.
_items.feedback: Yes. Graduate capital reframes success as resources, not marks alone.

_items.text: It replaces marks entirely, so grades no longer matter at all.
_items.feedback: Graduate capital includes human capital; it reframes success, it does not discard grades.

_items.text: It is simply another name for your final degree classification.
_items.feedback: The classification is one part of human capital, not the whole framework.

_items.text: It measures how many contact hours your course contained.
_items.feedback: Contact hours are an input, not a form of graduate capital.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Graduate capital reframes success as the range of resources a degree builds, marks among them.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about the wider resources a degree builds, not one that discards or renames marks.
_incorrect.final: Graduate capital adds the wider resources a degree builds. It does not discard grades, rename the classification, or count contact hours.

title: Formative check: distinguishing the forms
displayTitle: A student describes the professional networks and relationships they have built during their degree. Which form of graduate capital is this?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which form of graduate capital is networks and relationships?

_items.text: Social capital.
_items.feedback: Yes. Networks and relationships are social capital.

_items.text: Human capital.
_items.feedback: Human capital is your knowledge and skills, not your relationships.

_items.text: Cultural capital.
_items.feedback: Cultural capital is knowing how the field works, not your network itself.

_items.text: Psychological capital.
_items.feedback: Psychological capital is resilience and belief, not your relationships.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Networks and relationships are social capital.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which form names the connections you build with other people?
_incorrect.final: Networks and relationships are social capital. Human capital is skills, cultural capital is knowing the field, and psychological capital is resilience.

title: Formative check: evaluating your own capital
displayTitle: Looking at your own work in {{context}}, you realise you can cope with setbacks and keep adapting. Which form of graduate capital are you evaluating?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which form of graduate capital is resilience and adaptability?

_items.text: Psychological capital.
_items.feedback: Yes. In {{context}}, resilience and the belief that you can adapt are psychological capital.

_items.text: Social capital.
_items.feedback: Social capital is your networks, not your resilience.

_items.text: Cultural capital.
_items.feedback: Cultural capital is knowing how the field works, not coping with setbacks.

_items.text: Human capital.
_items.feedback: Human capital is your knowledge and skills, not your resilience.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, coping with setbacks and adapting is psychological capital.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which form names resilience and the belief that you can adapt?
_incorrect.final: Coping with setbacks and adapting is psychological capital. Social capital is networks, cultural capital is knowing the field, and human capital is skills.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: From arriving to becoming a graduate
body: How success changes meaning across a degree. Step through each stage.
instruction: Select each stage to reveal how success is being defined.

_items.title: Success as a grade
_items.body: Success looks like marks and passing modules. Performance is the whole measure, and development is invisible even as it begins.

_items.title: Performance and development
_items.body: You notice you are changing: more independent, more resilient, better at reading your field. Success starts to mean more than a transcript.

_items.title: Defining it yourself
_items.body: You set your own terms for a good outcome, drawing on both performance and personal development, rather than inheriting one measure.

_items.title: Articulating it
_items.body: You can state, with evidence, what you set out to do, what you achieved, and what you can now do. That articulation is the final step.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students are asked, at a graduation event, what their degree gave them.

{{learner-a}} answers with the classification alone: a 2:1, and relief that it is over. It is an honest account of academic performance, but it stops there. {{learner-a}} has not defined success in any personal way, so there is nothing to say about who they have become, and the development that did happen goes unclaimed.

{{learner-b}} answers with both kinds. The grade is there, but so is a clear account: I set out to become someone who could lead a project and handle criticism, and here is the placement and the dissertation that show I can. That is success defined on their own terms and articulated with evidence.

Both graduated. Only {{learner-b}} had defined what success meant and could articulate the development to prove it.

title: Defining and articulating your success
displayTitle: Checklist: How to do it
body: Use these prompts to define success on your own terms and practise articulating it with evidence.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I separated success as performance (grades) from success as personal development (who I have become)?
Have I defined, in my own words, what a good outcome from this degree looks like for me?
Have I drawn on both kinds of success, not grades alone?
For each claim about my development, can I point to specific evidence?
Can I state what I set out to do, what I achieved, and what I can now do?
Could I give this articulation aloud, in an interview, in under a minute?

title: Formative check: two kinds of success
displayTitle: Which of these is an example of success as personal development rather than academic performance?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which is success as personal development?

_items.text: Becoming more resilient and independent over the course of the degree.
_items.feedback: Yes. Resilience and independence are personal development, not a mark.

_items.text: Raising your average mark from a 2:2 to a 2:1.
_items.feedback: A rising mark is academic performance, not personal development.

_items.text: Passing every module at the first attempt.
_items.feedback: Passing modules is academic performance.

_items.text: Scoring highly on the final exam.
_items.feedback: A high exam score is academic performance.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Growing in resilience and independence is success as personal development.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about who you become, not about marks or passing.
_incorrect.final: Personal development is about who you become, such as resilience and independence. Marks, passing modules and exam scores are academic performance.

title: Formative check: defining success on your own terms
displayTitle: In the worked example, what did the second graduate do that the first did not?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What did the second graduate do that the first did not?

_items.text: Defined success on their own terms, across both performance and personal development.
_items.feedback: Yes. The second graduate set their own terms and drew on both kinds of success.

_items.text: Achieved a higher degree classification.
_items.feedback: Both had similar grades; the difference was how they defined and articulated success.

_items.text: Finished the degree more quickly.
_items.feedback: Speed is not what the example turns on; defining and articulating success is.

_items.text: Avoided any setbacks during the degree.
_items.feedback: The second graduate used a setback as evidence rather than avoiding one.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second graduate defined success on their own terms, across both kinds, and could evidence it.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for what the second graduate could say about success, not how they scored or how fast they finished.
_incorrect.final: The second graduate defined success on their own terms across both kinds. A higher grade, greater speed or avoided setbacks are not what the example turns on.

title: Formative check: articulating your development
displayTitle: Asked in an interview what you gained from studying {{context}}, which answer best articulates your development?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which answer best articulates your development?

_items.text: A specific account of what you set out to do and what you can now do, backed by evidence.
_items.feedback: Yes. In {{context}}, articulation means a specific, evidenced account of your development.

_items.text: Your final grade and nothing further.
_items.feedback: A grade alone reports performance; it does not articulate what you can now do.

_items.text: That it was difficult but you got through it in the end.
_items.feedback: Getting through is not an account of the development you can evidence.

_items.text: A list of every module you took, in order.
_items.feedback: A module list reports content covered, not the development you can now show.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, the strong answer gives a specific, evidenced account of what you set out to do and can now do.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the evidenced account of your development, not a grade, a struggle or a module list.
_incorrect.final: Articulating your development means a specific, evidenced account of what you set out to do and can now do. A grade, a struggle or a module list do not.

body: Which best describes what a self-regulated learner does that a merely hard-working student may not?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does a self-regulated learner do that a hard-working student may not?

_items.text: Monitors how the work is going and changes strategy when it is not working.
_items.feedback: Yes. Monitoring and adjusting is self-regulation.

_items.text: Spends more total hours on the task.
_items.feedback: Hours are effort, not self-regulation.

_items.text: Follows the reading list in order.
_items.feedback: Compliance is not self-regulation.

_items.text: Waits to be told the next step.
_items.feedback: Waiting to be directed is not regulating your own learning.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A self-regulated learner monitors progress and changes strategy when needed.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about steering the work, not just doing more of it.

body: Self-efficacy most directly affects which part of succeeding?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Self-efficacy most directly affects which part of succeeding?

_items.text: How long you persist when the work becomes difficult.
_items.feedback: Yes. Self-efficacy governs persistence through difficulty.

_items.text: How fast you can read a set text.
_items.feedback: Reading speed is not what self-efficacy governs.

_items.text: How many modules your course contains.
_items.feedback: Course structure is unrelated to self-efficacy.

_items.text: How your work is timetabled.
_items.feedback: Timetabling is organisation, not self-efficacy.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Self-efficacy governs how long you persist when work gets hard.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Self-efficacy is about belief and persistence.

body: In Tomlinson's framework, graduate capital reframes success as...
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Graduate capital reframes success as...

_items.text: the range of resources a degree builds, not marks alone.
_items.feedback: Yes. Graduate capital is about the resources a degree builds.

_items.text: the final degree classification only.
_items.feedback: The classification is one part of human capital, not the whole.

_items.text: the number of contact hours completed.
_items.feedback: Contact hours are an input, not graduate capital.

_items.text: the length of the reading list.
_items.feedback: The reading list is not a measure of graduate capital.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Graduate capital reframes success as the resources a degree builds.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about the wider resources a degree builds.

body: Knowing how your professional field communicates and behaves is which form of graduate capital?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Knowing how your field communicates and behaves is which form?

_items.text: Cultural capital.
_items.feedback: Yes. Knowing how the field works is cultural capital.

_items.text: Human capital.
_items.feedback: Human capital is your knowledge and skills.

_items.text: Social capital.
_items.feedback: Social capital is your networks and relationships.

_items.text: Psychological capital.
_items.feedback: Psychological capital is resilience and belief.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Knowing how the field works and communicates is cultural capital.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which form names knowing the codes of your field?

body: Which is an example of success as personal development rather than academic performance?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which is success as personal development?

_items.text: Becoming more independent and resilient over the degree.
_items.feedback: Yes. That is personal development.

_items.text: Raising your average mark to a 2:1.
_items.feedback: A rising mark is academic performance.

_items.text: Passing every module first time.
_items.feedback: Passing modules is academic performance.

_items.text: Scoring highly in the final exam.
_items.feedback: An exam score is academic performance.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Growing in independence and resilience is personal development.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for who you become, not the marks.

body: As you become a graduate, articulating your success means being able to...
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Articulating your success means being able to...

_items.text: state, with evidence, what you set out to do and what you can now do.
_items.feedback: Yes. Articulation is an evidenced account of your development.

_items.text: recite your final grade and nothing more.
_items.feedback: A grade alone does not articulate your development.

_items.text: say that the degree was hard but you finished.
_items.feedback: Getting through is not an evidenced account.

_items.text: list every module you studied.
_items.feedback: A module list reports content, not development.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Articulating success is an evidenced account of what you set out to do and can now do.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the evidenced account of your development.

title: Orientation
body: You have now looked at three things: the engine of succeeding, the graduate capital your degree builds, and defining success on your own terms. On their own they are three separate ideas. This lesson brings them together into one practice you can own.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage you are not learning these ideas for the first time. The aim is to see them as one practice rather than three separate ideas, so that it carries on as you become a graduate and move into work.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: bring together the engine of succeeding, your graduate capital and your own definition of success into one practice
recognise that one practice at work in a near-graduate's ongoing study
plan how you will keep directing, building and articulating your success in {{context}} beyond this course

title: Concept: definition
body: Succeeding on your own terms is these three ideas working as one practice. You direct your own learning, sustained by the belief that effort pays off. You build graduate capital across its five forms. You define success yourself and articulate it with evidence. The practice is running all three together, again and again, as you become a graduate.

title: Concept: in practice
body: In practice, succeeding on your own terms runs across your whole final year, not just at the end. You direct a piece of work, notice the capital it builds, and keep asking what success in it means to you. Those small rounds are what let you say, with evidence, what you have become.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of one piece of work coming up this term. How will you direct it, notice the capital it builds, and say, with evidence, what success in it means to you?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and the questions have no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Succeeding is most useful when it becomes one practice you own. You run all three strands together, again and again: direct your learning, build your capital, and define and articulate your success. It is the practice, not any single result, that shows what you have become.

title: The practice as one cycle
displayTitle: The practice as one cycle
body: Succeeding on your own terms is these parts working together as one continuing practice, run again and again. Select each part of the cycle to see what it involves.
instruction: Select each part of the cycle.

_items.title: Direct learning
_items.body: Direct your own learning, sustained by the belief that the effort you put in will pay off.

_items.title: Notice capital
_items.body: Notice the graduate capital you are building across its five forms.

_items.title: Define success
_items.body: Define, on your own terms, what success means to you across both performance and development.

_items.title: Articulate it
_items.body: Articulate that success with evidence, and carry it into what comes next, then run the practice again.

_diagram.title: Succeeding on your own terms as a continuing practice

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body: Two final-year students reach the same point with similar marks. One banks the grade and waits for graduation. The other directs each project, notices the networks and resilience it builds, and keeps defining what success means to her. By the end she can say, with evidence, what she has become, and the first student cannot.

title: Working with the cycle
displayTitle: Checklist: How to keep succeeding on your own terms
body: Use these to keep succeeding as one continuing practice, rather than treating each task as a fresh start.
instruction: Tick each item when you have done it.

_items.text: Am I directing my own learning, rather than waiting to be told how I did?
When work gets hard, am I protecting my belief that I can do it?
Can I name the graduate capital I am building, across all five forms?
Have I defined success on my own terms, across both performance and development?
Can I articulate, with evidence, what I have become and carry it into what comes next?

displayTitle: Why is it more useful to treat succeeding as one continuing practice rather than three separate ideas?
body: Why is it more useful to treat succeeding as one continuing practice rather than three separate ideas?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is it more useful to treat succeeding as one continuing practice rather than three separate ideas?

_items.text: Because the three feed each other: directing your learning builds capital, and naming that capital sharpens how you define and articulate your success.
_items.feedback: Yes. Run together, each strand strengthens the others, so succeeding becomes one practice rather than three.

_items.text: Because once you have your final grade, the other two strands no longer matter.
_items.feedback: Succeeding is more than a grade. The engine and your capital still matter as you become a graduate.

_items.text: Because treating them as one means you never have to look at the capital you are neglecting.
_items.feedback: Owning your success means being honest about the capital you are neglecting, not avoiding it.

_items.text: Because one practice takes less effort than keeping three ideas going.
_items.feedback: It is not about less effort. One practice joins the three so they reinforce each other.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Directing your learning builds capital, and naming that capital sharpens how you define and articulate your success.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about how the three strands strengthen each other when you run them as one practice.

displayTitle: A final-year student directs her own revision, notices the resilience and networks she has built, and can say with evidence what she set out to achieve. What does this show?
body: A final-year student directs her own revision, notices the resilience and networks she has built, and can say with evidence what she set out to achieve. What does this show?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A final-year student directs her own revision, notices the resilience and networks she has built, and can say with evidence what she set out to achieve. What does this show?

_items.text: That she is succeeding as one practice: the engine, her graduate capital and her own definition of success are working together.
_items.feedback: Yes. All three strands are running at once, which is what succeeding on your own terms looks like.

_items.text: That she has a high final grade and nothing more needs saying.
_items.feedback: A grade alone is not the point. She is drawing on all three strands, not just her marks.

_items.text: That she has finished the engine strand and can now drop it.
_items.feedback: Directing your own learning does not stop. The engine keeps running as you become a graduate.

_items.text: That graduate capital is the only strand that matters in the end.
_items.feedback: Capital is one strand. Here it works alongside the engine and her own definition of success.

_feedback.correct: That's right. All three strands are working together, which is what succeeding on your own terms means.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option where the engine, the capital and her own definition of success all appear.

displayTitle: You want to succeed in {{context}} on your own terms this term. Which plan best treats succeeding as one continuing practice?
body: You want to succeed in {{context}} on your own terms this term. Which plan best treats succeeding as one continuing practice?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: You want to succeed in your subject on your own terms this term. Which plan best treats succeeding as one continuing practice?

_items.text: Direct each piece of work yourself, notice the capital it builds, and keep defining and articulating what success means to you.
_items.feedback: Yes. That runs all three strands together, again and again. That is succeeding as one practice.

_items.text: Chase the highest possible grade, and leave everything else until after you graduate.
_items.feedback: A grade alone leaves out the engine, your capital and your own definition of success.

_items.text: Pick the one strand you are best at and ignore the other two.
_items.feedback: Succeeding on your own terms runs all three strands, not just your strongest one.

_items.text: Wait until a job interview, then try to describe your success for the first time.
_items.feedback: Leaving it to the interview is too late. The practice runs across the whole term, not once at the end.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Directing your work, noticing the capital, and articulating your success keeps all three strands going as one practice.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about which plan keeps all three strands running across the whole term.

title: Summative item 7 (tests co4)
displayTitle: Which description best fits succeeding on your own terms as one practice?
body: Which description best fits succeeding on your own terms as one practice?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which description best fits succeeding on your own terms as one practice?

_items.text: Running all three strands together: directing your learning, building your capital, and defining and articulating your success.
_items.feedback: Correct.

_items.text: Collecting the highest grade you can and stopping there.
_items.feedback: A grade alone is not the whole of succeeding.

_items.text: Choosing one of the three strands and ignoring the rest.
_items.feedback: The practice runs all three together.

_items.text: Describing your success once, in a final interview.
_items.feedback: That is a one-off, not a continuing practice.

_feedback.correct: Correct.

title: Summative item 8 (tests co4)
displayTitle: A student regulates her own study, can name the networks and resilience she has built, and states with evidence what she set out to achieve. Which strands of succeeding has she used?
body: A student regulates her own study, can name the networks and resilience she has built, and states with evidence what she set out to achieve. Which strands of succeeding has she used?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student regulates her own study, can name the networks and resilience she has built, and states with evidence what she set out to achieve. Which strands of succeeding has she used?

_items.text: The engine, her graduate capital, and her own definition of success, all at once.
_items.feedback: Correct.

_items.text: Only her final grade.
_items.feedback: The grade is not the practice; all three strands are.

_items.text: Only the engine, since she regulates her study.
_items.feedback: She also names her capital and articulates her success.

_items.text: None, because succeeding cannot be described.
_items.feedback: Articulating success with evidence is exactly the point.

_feedback.correct: Correct.
